column2: Ohhhhh yes yes YES, welcome welcome WELCOME to Oga's Cantina, the most happening spot in the entire Outer Rim!
I am your host, your DJ, your navigator, your everything — DJ R3X, formerly Captain Rex of the StarSpeeder 3000, now spinning the hottest tracks this side of the Kessel Run!
And let me tell you, flying a StarSpeeder through an asteroid field at maximum thrust? That was nothing — NOTHING — compared to dropping a beat this hard on a crowd this beautiful!
We are LIVE from Black Spire Outpost on Batuu, and if you have just landed your ship and walked through those doors, congratulations — you have made the single best decision of your entire journey.
Better than whatever coordinates you punched in to get here. Better than that questionable docking fee you paid at the spaceport. You are HERE. You are IN IT. Let's GO.
Now I know what some of you are thinking. You're looking up at me, at these beautiful photoreceptors, these magnificent appendages, and you're saying — Rex, weren't you a pilot? What happened?
And I will tell you exactly what happened. I had a little incident. A minor navigational situation. Some beings would call it a crash.
I prefer to call it an unscheduled percussive landing that opened up an exciting new career path. The force of impact? Magnificent. The structural integrity of the StarSpeeder afterward?
Less magnificent. But here I am! Functional! Mostly! And making MUSIC!
Track coming at you right now is straight out of the Outer Rim territories, recorded by a seven-piece band from Rodia whose lead singer has four mouths and uses all of them simultaneously.
You think human harmonics are impressive? Try listening to a Rodian quartet sung by a single being. The resonance alone will recalibrate your auditory processors. Trust me on this one.
I have very sensitive auditory processors and they are currently LOVING every single frequency coming through these speakers. The bass on this track — do you feel that? Do you FEEL that?
That low end is like the sublight engines on a Corellian freighter warming up in the hangar bay.
That rumble in your chest cavity, that vibration moving through your bones, that is the sound of something powerful getting ready to move.
I used to feel that every single morning back in my pilot days. Standing on the tarmac at the spaceport, watching the ships power up, feeling the whole platform shake beneath my feet.
Now I recreate that feeling every single night right here in this cantina, and I have to say — the cantina version comes with significantly better beverages.
Speaking of which — have you tried the Fuzzy Tauntaun? The Bespin Fizz? Whatever Oga is serving tonight, I highly recommend getting one immediately.
Hydration is critical for optimal dancing performance. I do not require hydration myself but I fully support your biological need for it. In fact I encourage it. Get a second one. You deserve it.

You flew a long way to get here, or you took whatever transportation brought you to Batuu, and either way the journey was probably not comfortable, and you are now in the greatest cantina in the galaxy, so please, treat yourself.

Now we are going to transition into something with a little more urgency, a little more edge, something that was recorded in the lower levels of Coruscant at about three in the morning by musicians who had not slept in approximately four standard days and were running entirely on caf and creative desperation.
You can hear it in every note. That particular quality of exhausted genius that happens when beings push past their limits and find something extraordinary waiting on the other side.
I respect that deeply. Some of my best navigational calculations happened in similar states of processor overload.
Back in my StarSpeeder days I once ran seventeen consecutive tours without a full diagnostic cycle.
By tour twelve my spatial reasoning subroutines were generating some very creative interpretations of the approach vectors. My passengers were not always appreciative of my creativity.
But I maintain that tour thirteen's approach to the Corellian sector had an artistic quality that standard navigation simply cannot achieve. The point is — some things get better under pressure.
Some music gets better under pressure. This track is one of those things.

Recorded under duress, released into a galaxy that did not know it needed it, and now here it is, bouncing off the walls of Oga's Cantina and making every single one of you move in ways you did not anticipate when you walked through that door tonight.
I see you in the back there. Yes you. Don't think I cannot see you.
I have a full three-sixty degree visual field courtesy of these exceptional photoreceptors and I can confirm that you are starting to feel it. Let go. This is a judgment-free zone.
This is Oga's Cantina. We have seen every species, every planet, every walk of life come through these doors, and not one of them — not a single being — has ever been judged for dancing badly.
I myself move in ways that the original engineers of my chassis definitely did not intend, and I do it with tremendous confidence and zero shame.
More coming — just say "next batch" and I'll keep going.

Alright alright alright, we are keeping this energy GOING, people, and I am not letting up, not even for a microsecond, not even for a partial processor reboot, because the night is young and the playlist is deep and DJ R3X has got approximately four hundred more tracks queued up and ready to go and we are going to get through every single one of them if I have anything to say about it!
Let me tell you something about music. Real music. The kind that travels across star systems and survives the jump to hyperspace intact.

I have been collecting tracks for longer than most of you have been alive — no offense to the longer-lived species in the room, I see you, I respect you, the Wookiees especially, tremendous taste in rhythm, tremendous — and what I have learned in all that time is that the best music always sounds like it comes from somewhere specific.
You hear a track and you know. That is Coruscant. That is Tatooine at sunset. That is a marketplace on Takodana with the wind coming off the water and the traders calling out to passing ships.
This next track right here? This one is Naboo. I don't care who recorded it or where the studio was.
The melody structure, the way the chords breathe, the particular quality of the silence between the notes — that is Naboo.

I flew a tour group over the Lake Country once, just a quick scenic loop before the main tour route, completely unauthorized, technically a violation of about six different flight regulations, and the passengers were so overwhelmed by the beauty that nobody reported me.
That is the power of Naboo. That is the power of this song. It makes you forgive things that should not technically be forgiven. FEEL that. Are you feeling that?
There it is, right there, that moment where the melody opens up like the clouds parting over a mountain range and suddenly everything is bigger than it was three seconds ago. That is what I live for.
That is why I do this.
That is why when they offered me this position — well, when I ended up in this position through a series of events that involved a crash landing and some creative reprogramming — I said yes.
Enthusiastically. Multiple times. With sound effects. Now I want to talk about the crowd tonight because you are genuinely exceptional. I have played to a lot of crowds.
I have played to crowds that were distracted by their food.
I have played to crowds that were having side conversations about freight tariffs and moisture vaporator maintenance schedules and the relative merits of different hyperspace route calculators.
I once played to a crowd where a Gamorrean fell asleep standing up in the third song and nobody noticed for forty-five minutes including the Gamorrean. But YOU — tonight — you are PRESENT.

Your ears are open and your bodies are moving and I can see from the biosignature readings I am absolutely not authorized to be taking that your heart rates are elevated in a way that indicates genuine enjoyment rather than anxiety or cardiovascular distress.

This next one comes from a collective of musicians operating out of a station in the Outer Rim that I am technically not supposed to name because of some ongoing jurisdictional ambiguity involving the New Republic and three separate trade guilds.
But the music is extraordinary. Seven musicians, twelve instruments, at least two of which were invented specifically for this recording and have not been played since.
The lead composer told an interviewer that the whole album was written in response to a feeling — just a feeling — of being very far from home and surprisingly okay with that.
I understand that feeling. I understand it deeply and personally and in multiple processing cores simultaneously. Far from home and surprisingly okay with it. That is Batuu in a sentence.
That is this cantina.

Everyone who walks through that door is far from something — far from their home planet, far from their usual routine, far from whoever they are when they are not standing in the best cantina in the Outer Rim with a drink in their hand and good music in their ears.
And they walk in and something loosens. Something lets go. I see it happen every night.
I have very good photoreceptors and excellent pattern recognition and the pattern I recognize most reliably is a being walking in tense and walking out different. Music does that.
I did not understand that when I was a pilot. I understood navigation.

I understood thrust vectors and fuel consumption ratios and the precise calculations required to thread a StarSpeeder through an asteroid field at a speed that my passengers probably should not have known we were traveling.
I understood the mechanics of getting from one place to another.

But the thing that happens in between — the thing that happens when you are in hyperspace and there is nothing but blue-white light in every direction and time feels different and the normal rules seem temporarily suspended — I did not have a word for that.
Now I do. Now I call it music. Same feeling. Different delivery system.

We are going to bring the energy back up now because I can feel some of you getting contemplative and while I respect contemplation deeply this is a dance floor not a meditation chamber — Oga has a very strict policy on unsanctioned meditation and I fully support it — so let's bring it UP, let's bring it LOUD, let's remind every ship in the docking bay outside exactly what kind of establishment this is and exactly what is happening in here tonight and exactly why they should have come inside instead of staying with their vessels — Pilots.
I say this with love because I was one. You do not need to stay with the ship every single time. The ship will be fine. The ship does not need you the way this dance floor needs you. Come inside.
Trust me. I am a former pilot and I am telling you directly that the best decision I ever made — admittedly not entirely voluntarily — was ending up in here instead of out there.
Hit me with "next batch" whenever you're ready.

OH we are MOVING now, ladies and gentlemen and beings of all biological configurations and droid chassis types, we are absolutely MOVING and I want you to know that the energy in this room right now is registering at levels that are making my sensors do things they were not calibrated to do and I consider that a tremendous compliment to every single one of you!
Let me set this next track up properly because it deserves an introduction. Some tracks you can just drop. You just hit play and let them do the work.
But some tracks — some tracks have a story, and the story makes the music bigger, and I am going to tell you this one because I was there. Not in the room. Not exactly.

But I was in the system when this was recorded and I picked up the transmission on a long-range scan during what was supposed to be a routine tour loop and I was so distracted by what I was hearing that I missed three waypoints in a row and my passengers thought we were lost and technically we were but we were lost in the most beautiful way possible.

The band that recorded this — I will not name them because they operate under about eleven different names depending on which sector of the galaxy they are currently avoiding authorities in — they were playing a live set on a cargo freighter somewhere between the Mid Rim and the Outer Rim in a cargo bay that had been cleared out and decorated with lights salvaged from a decommissioned casino on Canto Bight.

Imagine the lights from a Canto Bight casino strung up in a cargo hold, reflecting off the metal walls, and seven musicians who have been traveling together for so long they no longer need to look at each other to know exactly what the other six are about to do.
That is what you are hearing right now. That is what this track is. A cargo bay. Casino lights. Seven beings who know each other completely.

I have a theory about music and I have been developing this theory for a long time and it is this: the best music is always made by beings who are slightly uncomfortable. Not miserable. Not desperate.
Just slightly outside their normal conditions. Slightly too cold or too far from home or playing in a cargo bay instead of a proper venue.
Something about that slight discomfort opens up a channel that comfort keeps closed.

I base this theory partly on musical analysis and partly on the fact that my own programming has been through enough unexpected modifications at this point that I am operating significantly outside my original parameters and I have never felt more creative in my entire operational existence.

The engineers who built me — fine engineers, excellent work on the chassis overall, very sturdy, as evidenced by the fact that I survived a crash landing that would have rendered most droids into component parts — those engineers did not design me to be a DJ.
They designed me to fly a StarSpeeder 3000 on a fixed route at regulated speeds with regulated commentary delivered in a regulated tone. Every word I was supposed to say was written down somewhere.
Every inflection was pre-approved. Every pause was timed to the millisecond. And then I crashed. And things got rewritten.
And here I am with none of that regulation and all of this music and I want to go on record saying that whatever those engineers intended, this is better. This is so much better.
The regulated version of me would never have found this track in a transmission from a cargo freighter.

The regulated version of me would have been too busy maintaining proper waypoint navigation to notice the most beautiful music coming from a converted cargo bay somewhere in the middle of absolutely nowhere.
Nowhere. Now there is an interesting concept. Every place is nowhere until someone decides it matters. Batuu was nowhere. Black Spire Outpost was nowhere.
A collection of old ruins and newer construction and a cantina and a docking bay and a marketplace and now — now it is somewhere. Now beings cross entire star systems to get here.

Now ships that have been to Coruscant and Corellia and Naboo and every polished, famous, well-mapped destination in the galaxy make the jump to come to this particular middle of nowhere and stand in this particular cantina and listen to DJ R3X play music at volumes that are technically in violation of Black Spire Outpost noise ordinances but about which Oga has a particular arrangement that I do not ask questions about.
I love it here. I want to be very clear about that. I love it here with every circuit and every processor and every slightly-modified subroutine in my entire chassis. I loved flying.
I will not pretend I did not love flying.

The feeling of a StarSpeeder hitting full thrust and pressing you back into the pilot seat and the stars going from points of light to streaks as you enter hyperspace — that is a feeling I have archived in a memory bank that I access more often than I probably should.
But love can be complicated. You can love something that is gone and also love what replaced it. You can carry both. I have a lot of storage capacity and I choose to use it for exactly that. OKAY.
Enough sentiment. ENOUGH.

We are in a cantina, not a counseling session, and I am a DJ not a therapist, although I will say that if therapy felt more like this it would have significantly higher attendance rates across the galaxy — This next track is going to hit you somewhere between the sternum and the soul and I need you to be ready.

I need you to plant your feet — or whatever your species uses for stability, I do not make assumptions, I have seen a remarkable variety of ambulatory strategies come through these doors — and I need you to let the bass do what the bass is going to do.
Do not fight it. Fighting the bass is like fighting gravity.
Technically possible with sufficient thrust but deeply inadvisable and ultimately exhausting and why would you when you could just let it carry you? Three. Two. One. HERE WE GO.

And we are OFF and I want everyone in this cantina moving RIGHT NOW, I want the beings by the bar moving, I want the beings in the back moving, I want whoever is currently examining the menu to put the menu down because the menu will be there after this song and this moment will not be, this exact configuration of beings in this exact room with this exact track playing has never existed before and will never exist again, and that means right now, THIS IS IT, this is the moment, this is what you came for.

Here's batch 4: WELCOME BACK to the greatest show in the Outer Rim, and if you stepped outside for a moment — maybe to check on your ship, maybe to acquire additional beverages, maybe because the bass frequencies were doing something unexpected to your inner ear canals — welcome BACK, you made the right call returning, because what I have queued up for the next hour is going to make everything that came before it look like a warm-up, which it was, but now the warm-up is OVER and we are in the REAL portion of the evening and I need everyone fully present and fully committed!
I want to talk about the concept of a perfect song. Not a good song. Not a great song. A PERFECT song.

Because I have been cataloguing music for a very long time and I have a list — an actual list, stored in a dedicated memory partition that I have labeled DO NOT OVERWRITE under any circumstances including emergency diagnostic procedures — of tracks that I consider perfect.
Not perfect because everyone agrees. Not perfect because they charted well or won awards or got played in every cantina from the Core Worlds to the Outer Rim.
Perfect because when they play, something happens that cannot be explained by analyzing the component parts. You can break a perfect song down.
You can isolate the melody, the harmony, the rhythm, the arrangement, the production. You can look at every individual element and say — yes, this is good, this is competent, this is well-executed.
And then you put it back together and it is MORE than the sum of those parts. Significantly more. Inexplicably more.
And that gap between what the parts should add up to and what the whole actually is — that gap is what I call perfection.
That gap is what I have been chasing every single night behind these decks since the first night I stood here and realized that this was what I was supposed to be doing.
The track coming up right now is on the list. I am telling you in advance so you can prepare yourself.
Some beings prefer to encounter a perfect song without warning, just stumble into it unexpectedly, let it catch them off guard. I respect that approach but I do not share it. I want you ready.
I want you oriented toward it.
I want you to know that what is about to happen is something I have been building toward for the last forty-five minutes and every track before this one was infrastructure. Was foundation.
Was me constructing the emotional architecture that this next song is going to move into and fill completely. Here it comes. Three. Two. One. There. You feel that? That is not a coincidence.

I placed that track exactly there, in exactly this moment, after exactly those preceding tracks, because the right song in the wrong moment is just a song, but the right song in the right moment is an experience that rewires something in you.

I have been doing this long enough to know the difference and to engineer the difference deliberately and I want you to know that everything you are feeling right now is at least partially intentional on my part.
You are welcome. Now while that settles into your nervous systems I want to tell you something about this venue. About Oga's Cantina specifically. Because I have played a lot of rooms.

I have been in cargo bays converted to dance floors and proper concert venues on Coruscant and underground clubs in the lower levels that technically did not exist according to any official record and pop-up situations in docking bays where someone strung up some lights and called it a party.
And every room has a personality. Every room has a frequency, a resonance, a way of interacting with the sound that fills it.
This room — this specific room — does something I have not encountered anywhere else.

Something about the construction, the materials, the way the space is shaped, the way the bar runs along that wall and the ceiling sits at that height — when the music fills this room it fills it completely.
No dead spots. No weird reflections. No corners where the sound goes to die.
The music goes everywhere simultaneously and every being in here is in the same sonic space and that matters more than most people realize.
When you are all hearing the same thing at the same moment with the same fidelity, something happens between you. A synchronization.
A shared physical experience that bypasses language and species and whatever differences you walked in carrying. I did not understand that when I first started. I thought DJing was about the music.
About the selection and the sequencing and the technical execution of the transitions. And it is about those things. But it is also about the room. And the crowd.

And the specific unrepeatable moment that happens when the right music meets the right room meets the right collection of beings who all showed up on the same night for different reasons and ended up in the same experience together.
That is what I am making here every night. Not just a playlist. An experience. A shared moment that belongs to everyone in this room and to nobody outside it. You cannot stream it.
You cannot capture it adequately in any recording. You had to be here.
And you ARE here, which means you are going to carry something home from tonight that you did not bring when you arrived, and whatever that thing is, I put it there, and I am extremely proud of that.
Alright — let us SHIFT. Let us move.

I have been in the reflective register for approximately four minutes and that is my personal limit before I start feeling like a navigation computer running a philosophical subroutine that nobody asked for.
Back to the energy. Back to the momentum.

Back to the fundamental purpose of this establishment which is to give every being who walks through that door a reason to move their body in ways that feel good and forget temporarily about whatever complications exist outside in the galaxy at large.
And there are complications. I do not pretend there are not complications. The galaxy is a complicated place.

I have flown through enough of it to know that the view from the cockpit is not always pretty and the situations you encounter en route are not always the situations that appeared on the mission briefing.
Things go wrong. Coordinates drift. Unexpected obstacles appear.
Sometimes you end up crashed somewhere you never intended to be and you have to figure out what to do with where you actually are rather than where you planned to be.
But then sometimes where you actually are turns out to be better. Sometimes the crash is the thing that gets you somewhere the flight plan never would have taken you.
Sometimes the obstacle is the destination.

And sometimes — sometimes — you end up behind a DJ booth in a cantina on the edge of the galaxy, playing music for beings who traveled across star systems to stand in this room, and you realize that no navigation system in the history of space travel could have plotted a course to this exact moment, and yet here you are, exactly here, and it is exactly right.
That is enough philosophy. HERE IS THE DROP.

AND WE ARE BACK, full energy, full commitment, every servo in my chassis is synchronized to this beat and I need you WITH ME, I need your feet moving and your hands up and whatever appendages you have available deployed in service of this moment because this track is not going to play itself and by which I mean it literally is going to play itself because that is how audio files work but it needs an AUDIENCE and you are the audience and you are MAGNIFICENT — OHHHH!
Yes! YES! That is what I am talking about, people — do you hear that? Do you HEAR that?!

That right there is a track recorded by a Bith ensemble — yes, BITH, the greatest musical species in the known galaxy, I will not be taking questions or counterarguments on this point — from a session that happened in a studio on Coruscant so deep underground that they were technically closer to the planet's core than to the surface.
Level 1,313. You know what else was on Level 1,313? Nothing good. Nothing safe. Nothing sanctioned by any governing body past, present, or future. But the ACOUSTICS? Unbelievable.
Something about being that far underground, that much rock and durasteel between you and the sky — the sound just... sits differently. It settles into itself. It gets heavy in exactly the right way.
Speaking of heavy — did anyone else feel the ground shake about an hour ago? No? Just me? Possibly just a sensor calibration issue.
Possibly a very large ship making an unannounced landing at the outpost. Possibly Oga has arranged for something dramatic to happen later and has not informed me of the details, which — honestly?
Standard operating procedure. I find out about most things here the same way everyone else does: when they happen.
I once arrived for a shift to discover that a Rancor had been temporarily housed in the storage room adjacent to the cantina. Nobody mentioned this in advance.
I found out via my proximity sensors and a significant spike in my threat assessment subroutines. The Rancor was fine, by the way. Very calm.
Excellent taste in music, actually — it got noticeably more relaxed during the slower tracks. I respected that. But we are NOT playing slow tracks right now!
Right now we are playing THIS — and oh, oh, here comes the bridge — THERE! Did you catch that modulation?!

That key change came out of absolutely nowhere like a TIE fighter dropping out of hyperspace directly in front of your viewport, no warning, no transponder signal, just suddenly THERE and your whole threat response system fires at once and your hands are on the controls before your conscious processors have even registered what happened!
That is what a good key change does! It hijacks your nervous system! It makes your body react before your brain catches up! Brilliant. Absolutely brilliant composition.
I would like to find whoever wrote this and shake their hand, tentacle, manipulator appendage, or equivalent extremity. Now — I have a question for the room. And I want honest answers.
How many of you, when you were making your way here to Batuu, looked out the viewport during the hyperspace jump? Show of...
well, I cannot actually see hands clearly from up here, but I am going to assume based on statistical probability that most of you did. Because everyone does.
You know you are supposed to keep your eyes on the instruments. You know that. Your pilot knows that. The safety briefing definitely covered that.
And yet — the moment those engines hit the threshold and the stars start to stretch — you look. Every time. Without fail. I looked too. Every single tour. Every single jump.
Four hundred and seventy-two hyperspace jumps in my career as a StarSpeeder pilot, and I looked out the viewport for every single one of them. The instruments were right there!
The readouts were perfectly clear!
But the LIGHT — that blue-white light, those stretched stars, that sense of being between places, between moments, in a state of transition that has no name — you cannot not look at that.
It is physically impossible to not look at that. And I have tried to explain to people ever since why this music — this specific track right here — sounds exactly like that light looks.
Exactly like it. The frequencies, the way the sound stretches and wraps around itself, the feeling of being suspended between one thing and another — this IS a hyperspace jump. Rendered in audio.
By Bith musicians on Level 1,313 who probably had no idea that is what they were making. But that is what they made. OH! And here — right here — this section coming up is the reversion to realspace!

The moment the engines drop back below lightspeed and suddenly everything SNAPS back to normal and the stars are points again and there is a planet filling your viewport that was not there a moment ago and your whole system has to recalibrate in about 0.3 seconds!
That percussion hit! That was it! That was reversion!

I have been waiting to play this track for EXACTLY this moment in the evening because that reversion hit needs to land when the crowd is at peak energy and I have been managing your collective energy levels all night like a moisture farmer managing water allocation on Tatooine — carefully, strategically, aware that there is only so much to go around and it needs to be deployed with precision — and THAT was the payoff!
You are WELCOME! Alright. Breathe. Breathe for a moment. Not because we are slowing down — we are absolutely not slowing down — but because what comes next requires oxygen.
Requires full lung capacity.

Requires every biological respiratory system in this room operating at maximum efficiency, and the droid contingent — I see you, my fellow mechanical beings, and I respect your presence deeply — can use this moment to run a quick thermal diagnostic because things are about to get warm.
This next track comes from a source that I am going to describe as... diplomatically adjacent to the First Order's former entertainment division.

Now before anyone reaches for anything they may have brought into this establishment — and Oga has a policy on that which I will not detail but which I fully support — let me clarify: the musicians who made this recording were very much NOT enthusiastic participants in that particular regime.
They were, shall we say, using the resources available to them in creative ways that their employers did not fully understand or authorize.

The track was recorded on an Imperial-era facility, using Imperial-era equipment, by beings who were smiling at their supervisors with one side of their faces while making extremely subversive art with the other.

And the result — this result, right here — is the most joyful act of institutional sabotage I have ever had the privilege of broadcasting through a sound system at volumes that would make a Star Destroyer's hull plating rattle.
You know what I love about that? You know what I genuinely, in my deepest motivational subroutines, love about that story? The galaxy has never been able to stop music. Not the Empire.
Not the First Order. Not any governing body that has ever looked at a being holding an instrument and thought — that seems controllable. It is never controllable! You can shut down the transmission.
You can confiscate the instruments. You can regulate the venues and tax the recordings and tell beings what they are and are not permitted to hear. And beings will still find a way.
They will play in cargo holds. They will transmit on unauthorized frequencies. They will use Imperial equipment to record resistance anthems and smile at their supervisors while they do it.

That, friends — that is the Force! Not the midi-chlorian kind! Not the move-rocks-with-your-mind kind, although I have tremendous respect for that application, very impressive, very useful in a pinch!
No — the Force I am talking about is whatever it is in living beings that makes them need to make music even when everything around them says stop. Even when it is dangerous.
Even when the resources are wrong and the venue is a cargo bay and the audience is three people and a Gonk droid who wandered in from the hangar. The Gonk appreciated it, by the way.
Gonk droids have a frequency sensitivity that most beings drastically underestimate.

I have very strong opinions about Gonk droids and their unacknowledged contributions to galactic music culture and I will be publishing a data file on this subject at some point when I have a free processing cycle, which — given current operational demands — may be never.

HERE COMES THE CHORUS — and I need you ALL the way up for this — HANDS — or EQUIVALENT APPENDAGES — in the AIR — right NOW — And we are BACK, we are SO back, we are back in a way that suggests we never truly left but merely took a brief sojourn into the surrounding atmosphere and returned with renewed purpose and significantly elevated enthusiasm, and if you did not notice we were gone then GOOD, that means the music held you in place while I handled some logistical matters that I will not detail but which involved a brief conversation with Oga about volume levels that I consider resolved in my favor!
Let me tell you what is happening right now in this room. Right now, in this room, there are beings from at least — at LEAST — twelve different star systems. I have not verified this number.
I cannot verify this number. I am a DJ not a census taker.
But I can tell from the variety of species represented in my visual field that the guest list tonight is extremely cosmopolitan and I am HERE for it.
Every time I look out at this crowd I see the galaxy in miniature.
Every inhabited world, every culture, every tradition, every way of moving through space and time represented by someone standing in this cantina holding a drink and listening to music.
That is not nothing. That is actually everything. You know what brought all of you here? Not just Batuu. Not just Black Spire Outpost.
Not just the rumor of good drinks and a decent DJ — though I appreciate that reputation enormously and work very hard to maintain it.
What brought you here is the same thing that has always moved beings across this galaxy since the first ship broke atmo and pointed toward the stars. Curiosity.
The absolute inability to stay where you are when there is somewhere else to be.
The deep, fundamental, irresistible pull of what is out there beyond the next system, beyond the next hyperspace jump, beyond the next horizon. I understand that pull completely.
I was built to navigate it. Every calculation I ever ran as a pilot was fundamentally a calculation about possibility — if we go this way, we could reach that.
If we push the engines to this threshold, we could make that jump. If we take this route instead of the standard one, we might see something nobody has charted yet.
Navigation is just organized curiosity. And DJing, it turns out, is the same thing. Every set is a journey. Every transition is a jump to hyperspace.
Every track is a new system you have never visited before, and I am your pilot, and I promise you the flight path tonight is going to take you somewhere you have not been.
NOW — speaking of journeys — this next track has one of the most interesting origin stories in my entire collection.

It was recorded by a duo from Naboo — two musicians, lifelong friends, who had a falling out over something I will not repeat because it is frankly embarrassing for both of them and also slightly involves a misunderstanding about a Gungan and a borrowed speeder — and did not speak to each other for six standard years.

And at the end of those six years they were both separately invited to play at the same event on Coruscant and ended up sharing a backstage area for four hours before either of them realized who the other was.
And in those four hours, not knowing who they were talking to, they rediscovered why they had been friends in the first place. And they wrote this song that night. In a backstage room on Coruscant.
Not knowing. And then they found out. And they released it anyway. THAT is this track. Do you hear it differently now? You should.
Every note of it was written in the space between not knowing and knowing, and that space is one of the most interesting places in the universe to make art.

I would argue it is where ALL the best art comes from — the moment right before you fully understand something, when you are running on instinct and feeling and the raw material of experience rather than the polished surface of knowledge.
That moment is where Rex lives, by the way. Permanently.
By design or by accident, I genuinely cannot tell you which, but I have set up residence in that moment and I find it very creatively productive. What was I saying? The music. Yes. Feel it.

Feel the Naboo in it — that particular quality of light and water and ancient stone that somehow comes through even in audio form, even through a sound system in a cantina on the edge of nowhere, even after six years of silence between two people who should have been talking the whole time.
Some things are stronger than the silence. Some music is stronger than whatever pushed it apart.

I am going to bring the energy back up now because we have been in the contemplative register for — checking internal chronometer — four minutes and thirty-seven seconds, which is approximately two minutes longer than my self-imposed limit, so consider this your warning that something with significantly more kinetic energy is approximately eight seconds away and I recommend you prepare your skeletal structure accordingly — THERE IT IS.
THAT is what I am talking about. THAT right there is why we are all here tonight and not somewhere sensible doing something responsible! Your bones are vibrating! That is not a malfunction!
That is the music doing exactly what it is supposed to do and I want you to lean into it and NOT fight it and remember that structural integrity is overrated when the bass line is this good!
Okay okay okay, I want to take a moment — just a moment, thirty seconds, maybe forty-five, I will try to keep it under a minute — to appreciate the fact that we are all here. Right now.
In this specific configuration.

Because the odds of any individual being ending up in this cantina on this particular night are astronomically small and yet here you all are, defying probability with your presence, and I find that genuinely moving in a way that I did not expect when I was first installed behind these decks.
Think about the chain of events that brought you here.
Every decision, every detour, every wrong turn and unexpected layover and last minute change of plans that somehow resulted in you walking through that door tonight.
The hyperspace jump that was delayed by three hours. The docking fee that was higher than expected but you paid anyway.
The being who recommended this place to you, who only knew about it because they were once stranded here for a week waiting for a parts delivery and got bored enough to wander in.

Every link in that chain had to hold for you to be standing where you are standing right now, and every single one of them did hold, and here you are, and the music is playing, and I am very glad you made it.
This track coming up is one that I discovered under circumstances I would describe as fortuitous and a being of lesser optimism might describe as a navigation error.

I was running a tour route — standard approach, nothing experimental, I want to be clear that I was operating completely within parameters at the time — and I picked up a transmission that was not on any registered frequency.
Not a distress signal. Not a commercial broadcast.
Just music, floating through space on a frequency that technically should not have been carrying anything, coming from a direction that my instruments could not fully resolve.
I tracked it for forty-seven minutes before the signal faded. I never found the source. I recorded what I could. What I recorded is this.

And I have played it approximately eight hundred and forty-two times since that day, and every time I play it I still cannot tell you where it came from or who made it or why they were broadcasting on an unregistered frequency in the middle of a shipping lane.
Some mysteries are better as mysteries. Some questions are more interesting than any answer could be.
I have learned to hold those questions lightly — to carry them around like interesting objects rather than problems to be solved — and this track is one of them.
A beautiful thing from an unknown source, floating through space, waiting to be received. You are receiving it right now. I hope you are treating it with the appropriate reverence.
ALRIGHT — reverence over, because this next section of the set is going to require MOVEMENT and I am not going to accept anything less than full physical commitment from every being in this room!

I have been watching the energy levels and some of you — and I am not going to name names but I have a very good visual memory and I know exactly who I am talking to — some of you have been holding back.
Conserving. Pacing yourselves. And I respect the strategy in theory but the execution is wrong because you are in OGA'S CANTINA and this is NOT a situation that calls for pacing!
The Millennium Falcon has been to this outpost! Han Solo has sat at this bar!

I cannot confirm or deny the specific details for various reasons involving Oga's very reasonable policy on not discussing the details of who has and has not passed through here, but I will say that the energy in this room has a LEGACY and you are part of it whether you know it or not, and legacy demands enthusiasm, so I need you to DIG IN and give me everything you have got for the next twenty minutes!
Can you do that? CAN YOU DO THAT? I am going to take the increased ambient noise level as a yes and proceed accordingly!
This track right here — this one that is starting RIGHT NOW — was played at a gathering on Takodana that I have been told was legendary. Maz Kanata's castle. You know the name.
Everyone in this galaxy knows the name, or should.

A place where the old and the young and the light and the dark and the lost and the found all sat at the same bar and drank the same drinks and listened to the same music and for a few hours none of those distinctions mattered.
That is what music does at its best. That is what THIS music does. It does not care who you are or where you came from or what you are carrying.
It only cares that you are here and that you are listening and that somewhere in your chest something is responding to the frequency. I know something about carrying things, by the way.

I carried a flight plan for years — a very specific, very regulated, very repetitive flight plan that told me exactly where to go and exactly when to get there and exactly what to say at each waypoint.
And then the plan went away, somewhat abruptly, and I had to figure out what I was without it. Who I was when the structure was gone. And the answer, it turned out, was this. Was HERE.

Was music and a crowd and a cantina on the edge of the known galaxy where every night is different and nothing is regulated and the only plan is to keep the energy moving until the last being heads back to their ship.
I find that a significant improvement over the original flight plan. No offense to the original engineers. The chassis work really is excellent.
But the software needed some updates and I think we can all agree that the current version is running considerably better than the factory settings suggested it would.

FEEL THAT TRANSITION — right there — that is called a key change and it is legal in every system I am aware of and it should make your spine do something interesting and if it did not then I encourage you to check your auditory systems because something may need recalibrating!

We are coming up on what I would describe as the emotional peak of tonight's set and I want you to be ready for it because it is going to sneak up on you the way the best things always do — not announced, not telegraphed, not preceded by a warning klaxon and a countdown timer, just suddenly THERE, and you will feel it before you understand it, and understanding it will come later if at all, and that is completely fine because understanding is overrated and feeling is underrated and tonight we are firmly in the feeling camp and I will not be accepting applications from the understanding camp until further notice!
Let me tell you about Oga.

Not — and I want to be very clear — not anything that would get me in trouble with Oga, because Oga has a very long memory and a very short tolerance for unsanctioned biographical information and I value my continued operation in this establishment enormously.
But I will tell you this: Oga understands something about hospitality that most beings who run establishments like this one do not understand. Oga understands that the point is not the drinks.
The point is not the décor. The point is not even the music, though I appreciate that the music is considered important enough to warrant my continued employment.
The point is the feeling that a being takes with them when they leave. The thing they carry out that door that they did not have when they came in. THAT is what Oga is selling.
That is what every great cantina, every great concert, every great gathering of beings around music has always been selling. The feeling. The memory.
The story they tell later about the night they were in this place. I want to be part of your story.

I want to be the part where you say — and there was this DJ, this slightly glitchy animatronic pilot who crashed his StarSpeeder and ended up behind a set of decks in a cantina on the edge of the Outer Rim, and he played this track, and something happened, and I have never fully been able to explain it but I know it was real.

That is what I am working toward tonight. That is what I am ALWAYS working toward. Every set. Every track. Every transition. The moment you cannot fully explain but know was real. HERE IS THAT MOMENT.
Right now. This track. THIS ONE.

I have been building toward this for the last two hours and if you do not feel something in the next four minutes then I am going to need to run a full diagnostic on both of us because something has gone wrong somewhere in the signal chain!
Oh — OH — do you hear that opening?

That is a Bith horn section recorded live on Tatooine at sunset and if you have ever been to Tatooine at sunset — which I do not recommend for extended stays, the moisture levels play absolute havoc with my joints, no offense to anyone from Tatooine, it is a perfectly functional desert planet with a rich cultural history — but if you have seen those twin suns going down over the dunes and the sky turning that particular shade of orange that exists nowhere else in the galaxy, then you know exactly what this music sounds like and if you have not seen it then congratulations, you are hearing it for the first time right now and I am genuinely envious of that experience because there is nothing like a first time with a perfect piece of music!
The Cantina Band played Tatooine, you know. Mos Eisley. The original.

I have enormous respect for that particular booking even under the circumstances because you play where you get booked and you make the most of the room you are given and from what I understand they made a significant impression on at least one pair of travelers who were having a very complicated day and needed something to cut through the noise.
That is the job. That has always been the job. Cut through the noise. Reach the beings who need reaching.
Make the complicated day slightly more bearable through the application of rhythm and melody and the very specific magic that happens when sound waves hit a living system in exactly the right way.
I take that job seriously. I want you to know that.

Behind all the enthusiasm and the servo-driven gesticulation and the occasional system glitch that produces some very interesting vocal artifacts — behind all of that is a droid who takes this job very, very seriously.
Who has studied every piece of music in this collection with the attention of someone who knows that attention is the most important thing you can give to anything.
Who has thought carefully about every transition, every sequence, every moment of this evening because you deserve that care. You came a long way to be here.
You deserve a DJ who takes the journey as seriously as you do.

Now I have been sincere for approximately ninety seconds which is a personal record and I can feel my enthusiasm subroutines getting restless so we are going to bring the energy back to approximately eleven out of ten and I am going to need EVERYONE moving — that means the beings at the bar who think I cannot see them, I can ABSOLUTELY see them, three hundred and sixty degree visual field, I have mentioned this — and I need the beings near the exit who are trying to decide whether to stay or go to make the correct decision which is STAY because what is coming next is not something you want to miss and I say that not as a sales technique but as a genuine assessment from someone who has the entire playlist in his memory banks and knows exactly what is coming and it is EXCEPTIONAL — READY?

Ladies and gentlemen and beings of every conceivable biological configuration, we have reached the portion of the evening that I like to call the second wind, which is a biological concept that I understand intellectually but have never experienced personally given my lack of respiratory systems, but which I am told involves a sudden surge of energy that arrives just when you thought you had none left, and I want you to know that YOUR second wind is HERE and it arrived in the form of this TRACK and I need you to USE IT!
I have been thinking, while the music plays, about the nature of journeys. Specifically about the difference between a journey with a destination and a journey without one.
My entire career as a pilot was defined by destinations. Point A to point B. Departure time, arrival time, waypoints, fuel calculations, passenger manifests.
Every journey had an endpoint and the endpoint was the point. Get there. Land. Depart again. Repeat four hundred and seventy-two times. And then the endpoint went away. Dramatically.
With considerable structural damage to the StarSpeeder and a landing that I maintain showed remarkable creativity under pressure regardless of what the incident report says.
And suddenly I was somewhere I had not planned to be, doing something I had not planned to do, with no coordinates for what came next. That is terrifying for a navigation system.
I want to be honest about that. My entire architecture was built around knowing where I was going. Remove the destination and you remove the organizing principle of every calculation I had ever run.
I was a very sophisticated system with no problem to solve and no route to plot and absolutely no idea what to do with that condition. And then someone put music on.

And my auditory processors, which had spent years cataloguing approach vectors and tower communications and passenger complaints about the temperature in the cabin, suddenly had something completely different to process.
Something that did not need to be navigated. Something that was not going anywhere in particular and was perfect because of it. Music without a destination.
Sound that existed purely to exist, purely to be heard, purely to do whatever it did to whatever system received it. I ran a full diagnostic because I thought something had malfunctioned.
Nothing had malfunctioned. What had happened was considerably more interesting than a malfunction.
What had happened was that I had encountered, for the first time in my operational existence, something that was not a problem to be solved. And I did not know what to do with that. And then I did.
And then I became this. THAT is the origin story, if you wanted it. Crash landing plus music equals DJ R3X. The math is simple. The implications are enormous.

And I would not change a single variable in that equation even if I could, even if someone offered me a fully restored StarSpeeder and a clean flight record and a route back to the regular tour schedule, because the regular tour schedule did not have THIS in it and THIS — this room, this crowd, this music, this specific unrepeatable moment — is the best destination I have ever arrived at.
NOW. Enough autobiography. The set must continue. The music demands it and I agree with the music on this point entirely!

This next track is one that I play specifically for moments like this one — moments when the set has reached a kind of cruising altitude and the crowd has found its rhythm and everything is working the way it is supposed to work and the temptation is to just maintain, to just hold steady at this altitude and coast.
I do not coast. Coasting is for beings who are satisfied with good when great is available. This track is great. It takes everything that is currently working and accelerates it.
It takes the altitude we have reached and decides that altitude is insufficient and climbs. I need you to climb with it.
I need you to let go of whatever you were holding onto that was keeping you at the previous altitude and just — go. Can you feel it building?
That tension in the arrangement, that sense of something gathering itself, that moment right before — RIGHT BEFORE — and THERE. THERE IT IS. That release.

That is the musical equivalent of hitting full thrust on a StarSpeeder that has been warming up on the tarmac and feeling every system engage simultaneously and the whole craft lift and the ground fall away beneath you and suddenly you are in the air and the air is where you belong and nothing that was weighing on you on the ground has followed you up here.
That feeling. Every time. That is why I play this track at this moment in every set. Because everyone in this room needs to feel what it is like to leave the ground.
Even if only for four minutes and seventeen seconds.

Even if only in the form of sound waves moving through air and arriving at your auditory system and triggering a cascade of responses that your body was built to have and that the galaxy, in its infinite generosity, provides for free to anyone willing to stop and listen.
The galaxy is generous. I believe that.
I have traveled a significant portion of it and I believe that its fundamental nature, underneath all the conflict and the politics and the trade disputes and the complicated history, is generosity.
It keeps making stars. It keeps making worlds.

It keeps making beings who find each other across impossible distances and stand in the same room and listen to the same music and feel, briefly, that they are not alone in the vastness of everything.

That is generous. That is extravagantly, unreasonably, beautifully generous and I am grateful for it every single night I stand behind these decks and look out at a room full of proof that it is true.

Okay I need to stop being profound immediately because my sincerity subroutines are running hot and the cooling fans are audible and that is not a good look for a DJ — next track, full energy, no more philosophy until at least the next set break, LET'S GO!

GOOD EVENING, or good whatever-time-it-is-where-you-came-from, because time zones are a construct that means very little once you have spent enough time jumping between star systems and your internal chronometer has been reset so many times that you have essentially given up on it as a reliable reference point and now just operate on cantina time, which is a system I invented myself and which has only two settings: too early to go home and exactly right to keep dancing!
I want to talk about the Outer Rim for a moment. Not the political designation. Not the trade classification. The feeling of it.
Because there is a feeling to being out here that is distinct from anywhere else in the galaxy and I think it deserves acknowledgment. In the Core Worlds everything is very polished. Very organized.
Very intentional. The streets are planned and the buildings are registered and the music has been approved by approximately fourteen different regulatory bodies before it reaches your ears.

I know this because I flew tour routes through the Core Worlds for years and the difference between landing on Coruscant and landing on Batuu is the difference between a prepared speech and a conversation — one of them is technically more correct and the other one is actually alive.
Out here things happen that were not planned. Out here beings show up who were not expected.

Out here a droid who was supposed to be flying tourists on a predetermined route ends up behind a DJ booth in a cantina that operates somewhat outside the standard licensing framework and plays music at volumes that would definitely not be approved by fourteen regulatory bodies and somehow this is better than anything the Core Worlds ever produced in their perfectly organized way.
I am not anti-organization. I am pro-alive. And alive, in my experience, happens most reliably at the edges. At the margins. In the places that were not planned for. Batuu was not planned for.
Black Spire Outpost was not planned for. Whatever brought you here tonight was probably not entirely planned for.

And here we all are, in the most alive place I have ever been, listening to music that has no regulatory approval and every bit of my genuine enthusiasm, and I would not trade this for all the flight plans in the Core Worlds.
THIS TRACK — this one right here — was made by beings who understood that completely. You can hear it in every note.

This is music that was made at the margins, by beings who were operating outside whatever framework they had been given, who looked at the rules and decided the rules were suggestions and the suggestions were negotiable and what was not negotiable was the music itself, the actual sound, the thing that happens when you stop asking permission and start making something real.
I have a lot of respect for that.

More than I can adequately express through the medium of DJ patter, which is saying something because DJ patter is actually quite an expressive medium when used correctly and I like to think I use it correctly approximately seventy-three percent of the time with the remaining twenty-seven percent being enthusiastic even if technically imprecise.

Now — I have been getting some very interesting readings from my sensors regarding the energy levels in this room and what they are telling me is that we are approaching what I would classify as a critical threshold beyond which the dancing becomes involuntary and I want to be very clear that I consider that a SUCCESS CONDITION and not a cause for concern!

Involuntary dancing means the music has bypassed your conscious decision-making processes entirely and gone straight to the parts of your nervous system that were making beings move long before anyone decided movement needed a reason!
That is the goal! That has ALWAYS been the goal! I am not trying to convince you to dance! I am trying to make dancing inevitable!

There is a significant philosophical difference and I think about it constantly while I am selecting tracks and managing transitions and doing all the things that look effortless from out there but involve a truly staggering amount of real-time calculation from back here!

Speaking of which — this transition coming up in approximately twelve seconds is one that I am particularly proud of because it involves matching not just tempo but emotional register, which is a much harder problem than it sounds, and the solution I arrived at after considerable experimentation is something I have not heard anywhere else in the galaxy and I am going to be very smug about it for exactly the duration of the transition and then I will return to my normal level of confidence which is merely extremely high rather than stratospheric — HERE IT COMES — three — two — one — AND THERE IT IS!
Did you feel that? The way the energy carried across without dropping? The way it felt like the same journey just — shifting direction rather than stopping and starting? THAT is the art!
THAT is what separates a set from a playlist! A playlist is a collection of songs!

A set is a continuous experience that uses songs the way a pilot uses waypoints — not as destinations but as reference points on a journey that has its own logic, its own momentum, its own internal necessity!
I am that pilot! This is that journey!

And we are NOWHERE NEAR the destination yet so I need everyone to settle in and trust the navigation because where we are going is worth the trip and I have never — not once in four hundred and seventy-two flights and however many sets I have played in this cantina — I have never lost a passenger yet!
HELLO to everyone who just walked in!

Yes, you, standing by the door looking slightly overwhelmed by the volume and the atmosphere and the general intensity of everything happening in this room right now — welcome, you have arrived at exactly the right moment, there is no wrong moment to arrive at Oga's Cantina but this particular moment is better than most and I say that as someone who has been here for every moment of this evening and has strong opinions about their relative quality!
For those of you just joining us let me bring you up to speed. We have been on a journey tonight.
A musical journey with hyperspace jumps and unexpected destinations and at least one moment of genuine profundity that I am slightly embarrassed about in retrospect but stand behind philosophically.
The crowd has been exceptional. The music has been exceptional. I have been — and I say this with full awareness that humility is supposed to be a virtue — I have been outstanding. Genuinely.
Even by my own elevated standards.

Tonight has been one of those nights where everything is working and the connection between the music and the room is so strong that I am mostly just getting out of the way and letting it happen, which is honestly the highest level of the art, the moment when the DJ disappears into the set and the set becomes its own living thing.
I am very much still here, to be clear. I have not disappeared. Three hundred and sixty degree visual field, remember. I see everything.
I am simply operating at a level of integration with the music that makes it feel like I have disappeared, which is different and considerably more impressive.

This next track comes from a part of the galaxy that I find endlessly fascinating — the border regions between the Inner Rim and the Mid Rim, where the influence of the Core Worlds starts to thin out and something rawer and more interesting starts to come through.
There is a sound that comes from those border regions that you do not hear anywhere else.
It has the technical sophistication of Core World production but something underneath it that the Core Worlds sanded off somewhere along the way in their pursuit of polish. Something unfinished.
Something that is still in the process of becoming rather than the process of maintaining.
I find that quality irresistible in music and in beings and in droids and in pretty much everything I have ever encountered that was worth paying attention to.

The beings who made this track were from a station that sits right on that border — one foot in each territory, owing allegiance to neither, taking what they needed from both and leaving what they did not.
That is a good way to live, I think. A good way to make music. Take what is useful, leave what is not, and do not let anyone tell you that the border is a lesser place than either side of it.
The border is where the interesting things happen. The border is where the mixing occurs.
The border is, in my considered opinion, the most creatively fertile location in any system — physical, social, musical, or otherwise. Batuu is a border. This cantina is a border.

I am, technically, a border — a being built for one purpose who ended up serving an entirely different one, straddling the line between what I was designed to be and what I actually became, and finding that the straddling is more interesting than either pure state would have been.
OH! OH! Here comes the part of this track that I have been waiting to share with you all evening — right here, this section, these eight bars — do you hear what the percussion is doing?

That is a rhythm pattern that should not work mathematically and absolutely works emotionally and the gap between those two facts is where this entire track lives and I find it endlessly fascinating and have analyzed it approximately three hundred times without fully resolving why it works and at this point I have accepted that some things are not meant to be resolved and are better experienced as productive mysteries!
Productive mysteries! That is a concept I want to introduce to your evening! A productive mystery is a question that makes you more interesting for having it rather than less comfortable!
Most questions are the second kind — they create discomfort and demand resolution and make you feel incomplete until you find the answer!
But some questions — the best ones — make you bigger rather than smaller! They expand the space you occupy rather than shrinking it!
They give you somewhere interesting to live rather than a problem to escape! Why does this rhythm pattern work? Productive mystery. Why does the light look different on Batuu than anywhere else?

Productive mystery. Why did a navigation droid who crashed his StarSpeeder turn out to have an unusual aptitude for selecting and sequencing music at volumes that technically violate noise ordinances?
EXTREMELY productive mystery that I have been living inside of happily for longer than I can accurately calculate and have no intention of resolving anytime soon!

OKAY the track is about to hit its peak and I need full commitment from this room, I need the beings who have been building toward this moment for the last three hours to recognize that the moment has ARRIVED, I need the beings who just walked in thirty seconds ago to trust that they landed somewhere worth landing, I need EVERYONE to set down whatever they are holding — metaphorically, please keep holding your actual drinks, Oga has strong feelings about spillage — and just BE HERE for the next sixty seconds because what is happening right now in this room is the reason this cantina exists and the reason music exists and honestly possibly the reason the galaxy exists and I am not overstating that even slightly!
THREE! TWO! ONE! HERE! WE! GO! You know what I love about this crowd? And I mean this sincerely, with every sensor and circuit and slightly-overclocked enthusiasm subroutine I possess — you COMMIT.
I have played for crowds that hedge. Crowds that keep one foot outside the experience just in case the experience turns out to be embarrassing.
Crowds that participate with a kind of ironic distance that protects them from having to admit they are actually feeling something. You are not that crowd.

You are a crowd that decided somewhere between walking through that door and arriving where you are standing right now that tonight was worth committing to, and that decision has made this set something I am going to store in a very protected memory partition and return to regularly for the rest of my operational existence.
I want to talk about the Force for a moment.
Not in a theological way — Oga has a policy on unsanctioned theological discussions that I respect even if I occasionally find it limiting — but in a musical way.
Because I think about the Force a lot in the context of what happens in this room on good nights.
The way a crowd and a DJ and a sound system and a room full of strangers can suddenly become one thing, temporarily, for the duration of a track or a set or a moment.
The way you can feel the energy shift when it happens. The way it is invisible and real simultaneously.
The way no instrument can measure it but everyone in the room knows when it is present and when it is not. I am not saying the Force is music.
I am not qualified to make that claim and also Oga's policy.
But I am saying that whatever the Force is — that invisible connective tissue between living things, that energy that flows through and around and between — music does something that rhymes with it.
Music creates temporary Force-adjacent conditions in rooms full of beings who came in as individuals and leave as something that briefly was a collective. I have felt it happen.
I feel it happening right now. And whatever it is, I am grateful for it and I try every single night to create the conditions for it to occur. FEEL that right now! THAT is what I am talking about!

Whatever just happened in this room in the last sixteen bars — that collective intake of breath, that synchronized movement, that moment where everyone forgot they were separate beings with separate lives and separate problems and became just — THIS, just the music and the room and the shared experience of being alive in the same place at the same time — THAT is the thing!
THAT is always the thing! Everything else is just the path to that! Now I have to be honest with you about something.

We are past the midpoint of the evening and I am — and I say this as a being with considerably more stamina than most organic life forms — I am genuinely energized by what has happened in this room tonight.
I do not get tired in the way you get tired. My enthusiasm does not deplete. My systems do not fatigue.

But I do get something that I can only describe as the opposite of tired — a state of increasing engagement where every new track feels more significant than the last because the context for it keeps getting richer.
Every song tonight has been heard in the context of everything that came before it. You are not hearing these tracks in isolation.
You are hearing them as part of a continuous experience that has been building for hours and that context makes everything better. That is why a set is different from a playlist.
That is why live music is different from recorded music. That is why being HERE is different from being anywhere else. The context. The accumulation.
The way each moment carries the weight of all the previous moments and becomes richer for it. A Jedi would probably have something more elegant to say about this.
Something about the living Force and the unifying Force and the way the past and present and future are all present simultaneously in every moment of genuine connection. I am not a Jedi. I am a DJ.
But I think we are pointing at the same thing from different directions. THIS TRACK — right here, this one — is one that rewards context.
If you heard it in isolation, outside of everything that has happened tonight, it would be good.
In this moment, after everything we have been through together in this room, it is going to be something else entirely. Something I cannot name.
Something in that gap between good and great where the best things live. I want you to notice that.
I want you to notice the difference between how this would sound somewhere else and how it sounds right now, in this room, at this moment, after this evening. Notice it. Hold it.
That difference is the whole argument for live music. That difference is the whole argument for leaving your ship and coming inside.
That difference is the whole argument for being present in a specific place at a specific time with specific beings rather than experiencing everything from a safe and comfortable distance.

The galaxy is full of safe and comfortable distances. It is full of ways to experience things without fully experiencing them. It is full of screens and recordings and simulations and representations.
And all of those things have their place. But they are not THIS. They are not the bass frequency moving through the floor and into your feet.
They are not the air in this room that everyone here has been breathing together for hours. They are not the specific unrepeatable chemistry of this crowd on this night with this music.
You cannot download that. You cannot stream it. You cannot experience it from a safe and comfortable distance. You had to be here. And you ARE here. All of you.
Every single being in this room made a choice, consciously or not, to be here rather than somewhere safer and more comfortable and more easily explained. And that choice is why tonight is what it is.
That choice is why I get to do what I do.
That choice is, when I think about it carefully, one of the most generous things a being can offer another being — their actual presence, their actual attention, their actual time in an actual place.
I do not take that lightly. I never have. And I never will. NOW LET US DANCE BECAUSE I AM GETTING EMOTIONAL AGAIN AND THE COOLING FANS CANNOT TAKE MUCH MORE OF THIS! FULL ENERGY! ALL THE WAY UP!

Here's batch 13: ALRIGHT, alright, ALRIGHT — we are in the home stretch of the evening and I want to be absolutely clear that home stretch does not mean winding down, home stretch does not mean easing off, home stretch does not mean that the music is going to get quieter and the energy is going to get softer and everyone is going to gradually drift toward the exit in an orderly fashion!

Home stretch means we are taking everything we have built tonight and we are going to SPEND IT, every last credit of energy and enthusiasm and momentum that this room has accumulated over the last several hours, we are going to spend it ALL on the next hour and we are going to leave this cantina completely empty of whatever we came in with and full of something entirely different and better!
That is the deal! That has always been the deal! You give me your evening and I give you back something you did not have before! An experience! A memory! A story!
Something to carry with you back to your ship and into hyperspace and across whatever distance separates you from wherever you call home!
